strengths: UNOT addresses a useful problem: amortizing repeated entropic OT solves across datasets and resolutions. Combining Fourier neural operators, adversarially generated measures, and bootstrapped Sinkhorn targets is a meaningful contribution beyond dataset-specific amortized solvers.

The initialization results are promising. Table 1 reports reductions from 80 to 3 iterations on CIFAR and from 78 to 7 on LFW at the stated cost-error threshold. Table 2 shows approximately 2.75–3.4× speedups on the 64×64 datasets. Cross-dataset experiments, resolution sweeps, and the appendix’s marginal-feasibility plots strengthen this evidence.

For positive discrete measures, Proposition 5 provides a useful connection between the Sinkhorn fixed-point residual and dual-potential error through Hilbert-metric contraction. This gives a principled motivation for inexpensive bootstrapped targets.

The appendix provides substantial architectural and training details, pseudocode, and links to code and model weights. The barycenter and interpolation examples also suggest useful downstream applications.
weaknesses: The claimed generator universality is not established for the implemented method. Appendix C explicitly acknowledges that its 200-dimensional latent input, much larger output, and unenforced Lipschitz constraint violate Theorem 3’s assumptions. Consequently, that theorem cannot establish that this generator poses no coverage bottleneck. Furthermore, Corollary 4 is false as stated: with λ=1/2, G1(z)=ReLU(z/2) and G2(z)=ReLU(1+z/2) each satisfy the assumptions, but G2(G1(z)) is always at least 1 and cannot have positive density throughout the positive half-line. Although this corollary is ancillary to the implementation, it is an advertised theoretical contribution.

The OT formulations and potential conventions need reconciliation. Equation (1) has a negative KL term, whereas Equation (3) corresponds to positive KL regularization. Beyond this likely sign error, Equation (3)’s KL-reference potentials require marginal factors when reconstructing the discrete plan; the learned ε log(v) differs from that potential by ε log(ν), up to a constant. Proposition 2 therefore does not directly establish convergence of the quantity actually learned. Algorithm 1 also labels the transport-only cost ⟨C,Π⟩ as the regularized objective. These discrepancies obscure both the theoretical justification and the interpretation of reported errors.

The interpretation of Proposition 5 exceeds its guarantee. It bounds ground-truth error by a multiple of the residual; it does not establish convergence of the stopped-gradient adversarial training algorithm or equivalence of the two optimization objectives for a restricted network class. The constant can also become extremely loose at small regularization. The abstract’s claim should be narrowed accordingly.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed components or adequately establish state-of-the-art performance. There are no controlled ablations of adversarial versus fixed/random sample generation, or bootstrapping versus direct dual-objective training. Meta Optimal Transport is excluded because of dataset dependence, but matched fixed-resolution comparisons using the same generated data remain possible and informative. Gaussian-initialization timings are omitted because of implementation difficulties. The reported MNIST slowdown further shows that fewer iterations do not uniformly translate into faster solves.

Algorithm 3 is not a valid projected-gradient update as written: softmax(µ−gradient) changes a nonuniform probability vector even when the gradient is zero. Entropic mirror descent would instead involve log(µ), while Euclidean projected descent requires an actual simplex projection. The intended parameterization and implementation need clarification before the barycenter results can be reproduced reliably.

The claims about accurate transport plans and Wasserstein geometry rely heavily on qualitative examples. Figure 7 shows only one pair for the claimed superiority over GeONet, and barycenter and particle-flow experiments lack aggregate numerical accuracy measures. The marginal-feasibility plots are useful, but quantitative plan errors, barycenter objective gaps, and geodesic errors across many pairs are needed to support these broader conclusions.
